newsitem.title: USA: Minneapolis Fed sees good 1997 district ag outlook.
newsitem.headline: Minneapolis Fed sees good 1997 district ag outlook.

text.p: Grain growers in the northern U.S. Midwest should have another good year in 1997 while cattle and hog producer prospects improve slightly, the Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis said in its 1997 outlook.

"I think the fundamentals favor some improvement in wheat prices but I don't want to predict when that's going to happen. There's very little moving in the trade right now. It seems the major actors are holding off and waiting," Edward Lotterman, public affairs economist of the Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis, told reporters in a briefing on Monday.
Lotterman's briefing covered the bank's agricultural outlook for its district comprised of Montana, North and South Dakota, Minnesota, northwest Wisconsin and Michigan peninsula.

"The (grain) price signals that farmers got when they were planting were very high and made 1996 as intensive a year as you're likely to see. So I don't see large increases in grain output in this district in 1997," Lotterman said.

"The prospects for row crop states -- corn and soybean states Like Minnesota, eastern South Dakota and southeastern North Dakota, are quite good in income terms, the best they've been in several years, in 1997," he said.
Lotterman said the outlook was improved for livestock producers but still less rosy than for grain sales.
"There has been some cowherd liquidation over the past year. Beef output will not be growing. It will be down. The size of herds in this district is going to be lower," he said.

"The cattle states of Montana and the western Dakotas are still seeing very rough sledding. But we're past the price trough and prospects are improving. While 1997 will be better than 1996, it won't be great. But cattle ranchers should see some relief on prices in 1997 and increasingly in 1998."
"Hog output will be stable to perhaps slightly up in 97," Lotterman said, noting a trend to fewer, larger producers.
"We're seeing that trend. I think it will continue, but it won't be as accentuated here as it is in North Carolina. This is a transition, not a change that will take place overnight," Lotterman said.

"The environmental costs of hog production -- if there are and how much they are -- is one of the key political issues in South Dakota and Minnesota this year," he said. "The degree of difference in environmental regulations among the states is tightening up a bit. North Carolina is tightening."
North Carolina became the second largest hog producing state in 1993, from seventh in 1990, due to a rapid rise in the amount of "mega" hog farms raising 2,000-plus hogs.
Lotterman also said farmers can expect stable interest rates this year.
"Financial markets are integrated enough that small variations in demand for funds within the farm sector don't have that much influence on farm interest rates," he said.
"I see no reason now why there would be a large change in interest rates for agriculture through 1997," Lotterman said.
